episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Thursday, May seventh, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Leading off today's Innovation Pulse, thousands of schools and universities have lost access to the Canvas learning management system after a cyberattack during finals week. CBS News reports that the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for breaching Instructure, the company behind Canvas. The attackers exploited a vulnerability in Free-For-Teacher accounts and posted a ransom message on login pages across the country. Students at Penn State, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Columbia, UCLA, Northwestern, and the University of Chicago report being locked out of course materials, grades, and assignments. Penn State canceled all tests at its Pollock Testing Center Thursday night and Friday. The University of Texas at San Antonio postponed finals. The hackers claim nearly nine thousand schools worldwide were affected, with billions of private messages and records accessed. Instructure says it is working to restore full service, and school districts including Spokane, Washington are reassuring parents about data security. Canvas serves more than thirty million active users at more than eight thousand institutions and manages grades, assignments, lecture videos, and course communications.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In research news, a new study from Cornell and Carnegie Mellon universities found that A.I. tools are reshaping the college admissions essay in ways admissions offices may not expect. Researchers analyzed tens of thousands of application essays at a selective college and found that essay language became measurably more similar across all applicants after A.I. writing tools became widely available in twenty twenty-two. Students who received application fee waivers were more likely to use A.I. in their essays than other applicants. And lower-income students who used A.I. faced higher rejection rates than higher-income students who also used A.I. The findings, published by Inside Higher Ed, raise new questions about equity as A.I. assistance becomes a standard part of the application process.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to workforce development, the national nonprofit Advance CTE unveiled a new five-year vision for career and technical education at its spring meeting in Oxon Hill, Maryland. Education Week reports that the organization released a document titled The Connected Path, describing each student's educational journey as a connected series of experiences rather than isolated steps between school and the workforce. The announcement comes as career and technical education enrollment jumped ten percent in one year, from seven point eight million to eight point six million students nationwide, according to the U.S. Department of Education. At Riverside High School in Greer, South Carolina, students in an introduction to A.I. class are already presenting projects that use A.I. to boost agricultural productivity. The vision document calls for stronger coordination between K through twelve schools, community colleges, and employers to create what it describes as a co-designed system that works for learners and industry equally.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Meanwhile, community college faculty now have a free path to A.I. training through a new partnership between IBM and the National Applied A.I. Consortium. The consortium, founded in twenty twenty-four with National Science Foundation funding and led by Miami Dade College, has partnered with IBM's SkillsBuild platform to deliver customized A.I. learning for community college educators across the country. Faculty and staff can access more than one thousand courses covering A.I., cloud computing, cybersecurity, and data science through a structured pathway from foundational literacy to advanced hands-on labs. The collaboration supports IBM's goal of skilling thirty million people globally by twenty thirty, including two million learners in A.I. by the end of this year.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And court documents filed in the Elon Musk and Sam Altman litigation have revealed that the University of Michigan invested twenty million dollars in OpenA.I. during one of the company's earliest funding rounds. Business Insider reports that the university set a target redemption amount of two billion dollars on that stake. The investment arrived before Microsoft committed billions and before ChatGPT launched in November twenty twenty-two. OpenA.I. closed a one hundred and twenty-two billion dollar funding round in March at a valuation of eight hundred and fifty-two billion dollars. If the university holds its position through a public offering, the return could exceed one hundred to one, making it one of the most successful technology bets by a university endowment in recent history.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
